https://www.politico.eu/article/kyiv-for.text: NATO's reliance on the "doctrines of World War II" and its slow adaptation to new forms of warfare make it unlikely Ukraine will ever join the alliance, said Kyiv's Ambassador to the U.K. and former Commander-in-Chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi. "For 12 years, I must have personally been working to ensure that we mastered NATO standards, and every year I listened to tales that we were about to join NATO. Unfortunately, we will never join it," Zaluzhnyi privately told Ukrainian ambassadors in Kyiv on Monday, according to Ukrainian media. Although "Ukraine needs technologies that are still available in NATO countries today," like defenses against ballistic missiles, he said, "it is impossible to join an organization that possesses the doctrines of World War II with the level of development that exists in the armed forces of Ukraine." Advertisement Advertisement Russia has made deep changes to its forces under pressure from the war, and many politicians and intelligence officials worry it could be ready to attack a NATO country by the end of the decade. Zaluzhnyi's unusual rebuke underscores a growing change in the alliance's relationship with Ukraine. The country has shifted from relying on European military support in the early years of the war to becoming one the continent's most powerful and technologically advanced militaries — far ahead of Western forces in the mass production of drones, missiles and other key systems. "Ukraine contributes to transatlantic security," said NATO's 32 leaders in a joint declaration at the alliance's Ankara summit last month. In recent military exercises where NATO has invited Ukrainian troops to participate, allied forces have repeatedly been surprised by their tactics and drone use. The comments are also notable given Zaluzhnyi's widely rumored political ambitions. He was replaced as Ukraine's top commander by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in 2024. "Most likely, NATO will remain in the same form as it is, and will spend 12 years, like Ukraine, transitioning to the standards that need to be achieved in order to be at least half the level of the Russian Federation," said the retired general. Zaluzhnyi's remarks also reflect an enduring Ukrainian frustration with the alliance for stalling its application to join despite officially floating the prospect of eventual membership in 2023. The U.S. and other allies remain opposed. Advertisement Advertisement As a result, Zaluzhnyi said, Ukraine would instead opt to "be tied to blocs and alliances that will probably be formed," citing the Joint Expeditionary Force — a 10-nation U.K.-led grouping of mainly Nordic and Baltic countries established in 2014 and designed to complement NATO. "Most likely, we will talk about a European military security bloc," added Zaluzhnyi. NATO declined to comment, referring POLITICO to remarks made by alliance Secretary-General Mark Rutte in June, who reiterated the "irreversible path of Ukraine into NATO." Zaluzhnyi and Ukraine's mission to NATO didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Veronika Melkozerova contributed reporting from Kyiv.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c58j.text: Image source, AP Image caption, Agents arrested August Hanning (pictured from 2015) at his home on Tuesday By Olivia Ireland Published 2 hours ago Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says. Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant. Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved. Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money. Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage. Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near MÃ¼nster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday. Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration". "The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says. "On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient". Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years". Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block. Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies. State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents. It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia. Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly â¬400,000 ($450,000; Â£340,000). His trial is ongoing.
